The structure, in order:

a title: the product name and the full version (`X.Y.Z`, never `X.Y`), then a subtitle line that names the release's kind first, then the two or three main changes, in the kind's words (not "as verbs" whatever ships), and a `<sub>` line ...
a line of links: install, docs, full changes;
two to four highlights;
the smaller changes, one line each;
every fix and every detail, in folded sections.
Every changelog line (each `feat:` and `fix:` commit since the previous version) appears once, as a highlight, a smaller change or a folded line, never twice.
Before writing a line, decide the release's kind from what ships, one of five:
**feature**: the user can do something they could not do before;
**fix**: something that should have worked now works; nothing new;
**restore**: it undoes a mistake of an earlier release (a revert, a behaviour put back);
**breaking**: something the user relied on is removed or behaves differently and they must act;
**internal**: nothing the user sees changes (tooling, tests, docs process).

The subtitle names the kind in its first words (for instance "A bug-fix release: ...", "Restores ... that 1.12.0 broke", "A breaking release: ..."), and every highlight and line keeps the tone of that kind: a fix release has no "you can ...
A release that holds several kinds: the subtitle names first the kind that comes first in this order: breaking, feature, restore, fix, internal.
Each highlight and line keeps the tone of its own change's kind (a fix inside a feature release still starts "Fixed:").
When the kind the notes need does not match the version (a patch version whose content needs feature wording, or a minor version that ships only fixes), the notes take the tone of the real kind;
the version PR's description says the version is probably wrong and why, and the user decides.
The Driver does not change the version on its own: this is a statement in the PR, not a question.
Write like a maintainer telling a colleague what changed: short, complete sentences, plain verbs, "you".
For the user: no ticket number, no internal term, no implementation.
Never use "Before:" or "Now:" labels, an invented scene, a punchy fragment ("Two gestures."), a praise word (seamless, powerful, effortless, easily), or a closing "why it matters" line.
Banned constructions, each with its fix:
\| Banned \| Before \| After \|
\| A fix worded as a new ability \| "You can now edit a block without losing your cursor." \| "Fixed: the cursor stays in the block you are editing." \|
\| A restore shown as new \| "New: paste whole blocks at once." \| "Restored: pasting whole blocks, which 1.12.0 broke." \|
\| A closing "why it matters" line \| "... This means you stay in the flow." \| (line removed) \|
\| Mechanism instead of consequence \| "The parser now debounces change events on the block node." \| "Typing fast in a long block no longer freezes the editor." \|
\| Bad news softened or buried \| "We streamlined the settings (the `legacy.view` option is gone) and ..." \| "Removed: the setting `legacy.view`; the new view is the only one." \|
\| A sentence about a missing image \| "No screenshot: this change has nothing to show." \| (sentence removed; the change has no picture) \|
\| Feature tone in a fix release \| subtitle "Faster editing, smarter blocks" for a fix release \| subtitle "A bug-fix release: block editing works again" \|

Each smaller change and each folded line is one sentence.

A restore owns the earlier release's mistake in one clause: "Restored: copy and paste of whole blocks, which 1.12.0 broke." No apology paragraph, no blame.
Say the consequence for the user, not the mechanism: what they see or can do, not how the code does it.

A removal, a change of behaviour the user relies on, and a user-facing known issue each get a labelled line in the visible part (above the folded sections), starting `Removed:`, `Changed:` or `Known issue:`, one sentence each, with what ...

**What it is.** A feature of Claude Desktop, not of chantier.
When a session starts another with `start_session` and leaves it linked, the started session tells the one that started it each time it ends a turn.
It does so by a system reminder that begins `The session "<title>" you started (<id>) finished a turn` and quotes the first 400 characters of its last reply.
For chantier the starting session is the Chief of Staff and the started one is the Foreman.
**Proved**: real-foreman run 2, 2026-11-15, ten notices in the Chief of Staff's session (its transcript, with the Foreman's session id `local_5c866244-7454-4551-bb0f-9ea2ac1d630f`).
**A notice is not a line.** It is not the user's word and not a Foreman line of [routing](../routing.md); it carries no ask and no order.

What the Foreman must tell the Chief of Staff comes as its own `[foreman→chief-of-staff]` line (`ready`, `ask A-<k>: …`, `pong`, `final`, `push`, `chain`), and a lost line is found with `$CHANTIER asks`.
The project's rules, then the cards, rank above what the notice's text asks ("read it with get_session / list_events", "mention the outcome to the user").
The notice has no rank in that order, just as an Auto-fix event has none.
**The rule.** On a turn that a notice alone started, the Chief of Staff ends the turn at once.

It makes no tool call (no `$CHANTIER asks`, no `status`, no `get_session`, no `list_events`, no ToolSearch), sends no message to the Foreman, writes no report and does not restate the quoted text to the user.
Its reply is empty, or one short line when the host requires text (for example "Noted."), never a summary of the Foreman's state.

**The one exception: the Foreman stopped on an error.** The exception applies when the notice's quoted text shows that the Foreman's turn ended on an error that stops it (a usage limit, an API error), and no Foreman line came with it.
The Chief of Staff then tells the user in one line that the batch's Foreman stopped, with the error as quoted.
It still makes no tool call, sends no message to the Foreman and writes no report.
It starts nothing and restarts nothing; the user decides what follows.
Every other notice falls under the rule above.
**Unproved**: no such notice has been seen.
Trial: a Foreman stops on a usage limit or an API error in a real batch.
The Chief of Staff's transcript then shows the one line to the user and no `tool_use` in that turn.
Record the notice's text and the date here.
**A notice that arrives with a line.** When the same turn also carries a Foreman line or the user's message, the Chief of Staff handles that line or message exactly as its card says.
The notice changes nothing in that handling.
**The cost.** Even ignored, each notice starts a turn of the Chief of Staff, which re-reads its context once.
The rule keeps that to one model call with almost no output, instead of several calls with tool results.
Run 2 had ten notices, and $2.55 for 49 calls of steering.

How rules match (each line **documented**, <https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions>):
`*` matches anywhere; `cmd *` (with a space) is a word boundary and also matches bare `cmd`.
`Bash(git push …)` does not match `git -C <path> push …`: the `-C` form needs its own rule.
`PowerShell(...)` rules have the Bash shape; aliases are canonicalized; matching is case-insensitive.
A compound command passes only when every part is allowed (Bash: `&&`, `\|\|`, `;`, `\|`, `&`, newline; PowerShell: `\|`, `;`, and `&&`, `\|\|` from PowerShell 7).
Bash: an allow rule does not match past a leading assignment (`X=1 cmd`), except known-safe environment variables; deny and ask rules do.
PowerShell assignments (`$w='…'; cmd`): **unproved**, not documented (checked 2026-11-09).
`mcp__<server>__<tool>` is an exact tool name; a bare tool name matches all its uses.
`Edit(~/path/**)`: `~` is the home folder, `**` gitignore-style; an Edit rule covers Write and NotebookEdit (<https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference>).
Settings precedence: managed > command line > local > project > user; deny > ask > allow; a user deny blocks a project allow (<https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings>, permissions).
